lines.text: You tap your phone, and the coffee is paid. No cable, no battery in the card. So how does it work?
Inside the payment terminal is a coil of wire. And inside your card, or your phone, is another one.
The terminal pushes electricity through its coil, flipping thirteen and a half million times a second. That makes an invisible magnetic field.
Bring the card close, and that field makes electricity in the card's coil. Enough to wake up its tiny chip. That's why a card needs no battery.
To answer, the chip doesn't shout back. It just flickers how much power it takes, and the terminal reads those flickers as ones and zeros.
The field fades fast. A few centimeters away, it's gone. That's not a flaw, it's the point. You have to mean to tap.
And your real card number usually never leaves. The phone sends a stand-in number, plus a one-time code made just for this payment.
Steal that code, and it's useless. It already worked once.
NFC needs a tap. Orbi Transfer reaches phones nearby without touching at all, and locks every file before it leaves.
